title: Three jobs of the lymphatic system
summary: Start here from zero: the 30 L / 27 L / 3 L fluid budget, fat absorption as chyle, and defense by nodes and spleen.
objectives: State the three functions of the lymphatic system
Explain the 30 L / 27 L / 3 L numbers and what the leftover 3 L is called
Define lacteals and chyle
Say what lymph nodes filter versus what the spleen filters
takeaways: Fluid balance: 30 L of fluid leave blood capillaries into interstitial fluid each day; 27 L return to the blood; the leftover 3 L enters lymphatic capillaries and is called lymph.
Lipid absorption: lacteals in intestinal villi take up fat; the milky lymph is chyle.
Defense: lymph nodes filter microorganisms and foreign substances from lymph; the spleen filters them from blood.
The system is lymph, vessels, tissue, nodules, nodes, tonsils, spleen and thymus.

steps.title: Welcome to Chapter 22: lymphatics and immunity
steps.text:
Chapters 20 and 21 built a closed loop: the heart raises pressure, vessels carry blood, and capillaries exchange fluid with the tissues. This chapter answers what happens to the fluid that does not go back into the blood, and how the body defends itself against things that arrive in that fluid.

The lymphatic system has three jobs you must be able to list from a blank page: fluid balance, lipid absorption, and defense. Immunity (innate then adaptive) is the last half of the chapter. Each lesson assumes only the ones before it.

The atlas shows the spleen (left abdomen), the thymus (behind the sternum), the palatine tonsils and the lymph nodes strung along the vessels of the neck, axilla, chest, abdomen and groin. The atlas has no lymphatic vessels, so the drainage diagram in the panel carries the vessel story.

check.q: Name the three functions of the lymphatic system.
check.a: Fluid balance, lipid absorption, and defense.

steps.title: Fluid balance: 30 L out, 27 L back, 3 L becomes lymph
steps.text:
Blood capillaries leak. Every day about 30 L of fluid is forced out of capillaries into the spaces around cells. That fluid is interstitial fluid (IF).

Most of it, about 27 L, is pulled back into the blood at the venous ends of capillaries (blood pressure has fallen; plasma proteins still pull water in by osmosis).

The leftover 3 L does not re-enter blood capillaries. It enters lymphatic capillaries and is then called lymph. Lymph is returned to the blood in the great veins of the thorax, so you do not slowly drown in your own tissue fluid.

Memorize 30 / 27 / 3. It is a favourite exam stem, and it is why this system exists.

Course model: 30/27/3 is the supplied lecture’s traditional fluid budget. Modern microvascular physiology places greater emphasis on lymphatic return and does not assume sustained venous-end reabsorption in every tissue.
steps.pitfall: Lymph is not a separate fluid made from scratch. It is leftover interstitial fluid that entered a lymphatic capillary.

check.q: How much fluid leaves blood capillaries each day, how much returns, and what is the leftover called?
check.a: 30 L leaves, 27 L returns to blood, 3 L becomes lymph.

steps.title: What lymph is, and the parts of the system
steps.text:
Lymph is the fluid inside lymphatic vessels: clear (except after a fatty meal, when intestinal lymph is milky). It carries water, small solutes, some protein, lymphocytes, and anything that leaked from the tissues, including microbes.

The anatomy list for this chapter is short. Learn the names now; later lessons fill each one in.

Lymph (the fluid). Lymphatic vessels (the pipes). Lymphatic tissue and lymphatic nodules (diffuse and dense collections of lymphocytes, many of them in mucous membranes). Tonsils (groups of nodules, not fully encapsulated). The organs with a capsule: lymph nodes, spleen and thymus.

check.q: List the parts of the lymphatic system named in lecture.
check.a: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, lymphatic tissue, lymphatic nodules, lymph nodes, tonsils, spleen, thymus.

steps.title: Lipid absorption: lacteals and chyle
steps.text:
Dietary fat does not go straight into blood capillaries of the gut (those capillaries take water-soluble nutrients to the hepatic portal vein). Fat and other lipid-soluble substances are taken up by special lymphatic capillaries inside intestinal villi called lacteals.

The lymph in lacteals is milky because it is full of fat droplets. That milky lymph is called chyle.

Chyle is carried through intestinal lymphatics into the intestinal trunk and then, with the rest of the body's lymph, back to the blood. After a fatty meal the thoracic-duct lymph looks like milk; that is chyle arriving in the veins.

The atlas shows the small intestine as a whole; the ileum is not a separate atlas piece. The ileum slide shows villi, each with its central lacteal.
steps.mnemonic: Lacteal sounds like lact- (milk). The fluid is chyle (from the Greek for juice).

check.q: What is a lacteal, and what is chyle?
check.a: A lacteal is a lymphatic capillary in an intestinal villus that absorbs fat. Chyle is the milky lymph in those vessels.

steps.title: Defense: nodes filter lymph, spleen filters blood
steps.text:
The third job is defense. Microorganisms and foreign substances are filtered from lymph by lymph nodes and filtered from blood by the spleen.

That pairing is an exam discriminator. Lymph nodes sit on lymphatic vessels, so they see what came from the tissues in lymph. The spleen sits on the blood stream, so it sees what is circulating in blood.

Find the spleen in the left upper abdomen, tucked under the ribs. The liver is shown because Kupffer cells there also clean blood, but the lecture's named blood filter for this chapter is the spleen.
steps.pitfall: Do not swap them. Nodes filter LYMPH. The spleen filters BLOOD.

check.q: What do lymph nodes filter, and what does the spleen filter?
check.a: Nodes filter lymph; the spleen filters blood.

steps.title: Where you will look next
steps.text:
Order of the chapter: vessels (how lymph is collected and moved) → trunks and ducts (which side of the body drains where) → tissues and organs (primary vs secondary, MALT) → nodes, spleen, thymus, tonsils, Peyer patches → then innate immunity (barriers, chemicals, white cells) → adaptive immunity (antigens, MHC, clones, antibodies, T cells, acquired immunity, aging).

If you only remember one number-set from this lesson, make it 30 L / 27 L / 3 L.

check.q: Why does leftover interstitial fluid have to enter lymphatic capillaries?
check.a: Because the 3 L that does not return to blood capillaries would accumulate in the tissues; lymphatics return it to the blood.

practice.q: About how much fluid leaves blood capillaries into the tissues each day?
practice.why: Lecture: 30 L from capillaries into interstitial fluid; 27 L return; 3 L becomes lymph.

practice.q: The leftover 3 L of interstitial fluid that enters lymphatic capillaries is called…
practice.why: Once interstitial fluid enters a lymphatic capillary it is called lymph. Chyle is specifically milky intestinal lymph.

practice.q: Lacteals absorb fat in which structures?
practice.why: Lacteals are lymphatic capillaries of intestinal villi.

practice.q: Milky lymph from the gut is called…
practice.why: Chyle is fat-rich lymph in lacteals. Chyme is stomach contents.

practice.q: Lymph nodes filter microorganisms from…
practice.why: Nodes filter lymph. The spleen filters blood.

practice.q: The spleen filters microorganisms from…
practice.why: Spleen filters blood; nodes filter lymph.

practice.q: State the 30 / 27 / 3 fluid budget.
practice.a: 30 L leaves blood capillaries into IF; 27 L returns to blood; 3 L becomes lymph.

practice.q: Name the three functions of the lymphatic system.
practice.a: Fluid balance, lipid absorption, and defense.

practice.q: Put the fluid names in the order they occur, starting in the blood capillary.

title: Lymphatic capillaries and how lymph is moved
summary: Why lymphatic capillaries leak in one direction, where they are absent, and how lymph moves without a heart of its own.
objectives: Contrast lymphatic capillaries with blood capillaries (permeability, basement membrane, one-way flaps)
List the tissues that lack lymphatic capillaries
Describe the valves of lymphatic vessels
Name the three ways lymph is moved toward the heart
takeaways: Lymphatic capillaries are more permeable than blood capillaries and lack a basement membrane; overlapping endothelial cells act as one-way flaps.
Absent from nervous system, bone marrow, and avascular tissues: cartilage, cornea, epidermis.
Superficial lymphatics follow veins; deep lymphatics follow arteries. Vessels resemble small veins and have valves.
No central pump. Movement: vessel-wall contraction (pacemaker cells in chamber smooth muscle), skeletal-muscle compression, thoracic pressure changes.

steps.title: From tissue fluid into a lymphatic capillary
steps.text:
Lymphatic vessels carry lymph away from tissues (never toward them). The smallest vessels are lymphatic capillaries.

They are more permeable than blood capillaries and they lack a basement membrane. Their endothelium is arranged as a series of overlapping cells that work as one-way valves (flaps). When interstitial pressure is higher than the pressure inside, the flaps are pushed open and fluid (plus cells and debris) enters. When pressure inside is higher, the flaps are pushed shut, so lymph cannot leak back into the tissue.

On the capillary model, find the green lymphatic capillary below the blood capillaries: its blind end, the overlapping endothelial cells whose free edges act as the flaps, and the anchoring filaments that tie it to the collagen fibres. When the tissue swells with fluid, the filaments pull the capillary open.
steps.pitfall: Blood capillaries have a basement membrane. Lymphatic capillaries do not, which is part of why they are so leaky in one direction.

check.q: Name two structural reasons lymphatic capillaries take up interstitial fluid so easily.
check.a: They are more permeable than blood capillaries, and they lack a basement membrane; overlapping endothelial flaps act as one-way valves.

steps.title: Where lymphatic capillaries are absent
steps.text:
They are almost everywhere there are blood vessels, with important exceptions you must list.

Nervous system. These are tissue categories, rather than separate structures to identify in the viewer.

Bone marrow. Red marrow is one of the exceptions. Marrow has no lymphatic capillaries.

Tissues without blood vessels: cartilage, cornea, and epidermis. No blood vessels means no lymphatics either.

Elsewhere they form two sets: superficial lymphatics (they follow veins) and deep lymphatics (they follow arteries). Capillaries join to form lymphatic vessels.

check.q: List the places lymphatic capillaries are absent.
check.a: Nervous system, bone marrow, and avascular tissues: cartilage, cornea, and epidermis.

steps.title: Lymphatic vessels look like small veins
steps.text:
Once capillaries have joined, the tubes are called lymphatic vessels. Their wall is like a small vein: thin, with some smooth muscle, and (the important part) valves that ensure one-way flow.

Valves divide each vessel into a series of short chambers. Lymph can go toward the heart; it cannot go backward. That is why a blocked or damaged lymphatic looks swollen distal to the block: fluid can enter but cannot pass the obstruction.

Lymph nodes sit along these vessels and filter the lymph before it is returned to blood (next lessons).

On the model, the lymphatic capillary drains into a collecting lymphatic vessel; inside it, find the two-leaflet valve.

check.q: What do lymphatic vessels resemble, and what do their valves do?
check.a: They resemble small veins. Valves ensure one-way flow of lymph toward the heart.

steps.title: There is no lymphatic heart
steps.text:
Blood has the heart. Lymph has no central pump. Three mechanisms move it.

1. Contraction of the lymphatic vessels themselves. The unidirectional valves divide a vessel into chambers that act as pumps. Smooth muscle in the chamber walls contains pacemaker cells, so the vessel can squeeze on its own, chamber by chamber, pushing lymph toward the next valve.

That is intrinsic pumping, analogous in spirit (not in anatomy) to the heart's pacemaker, but it is in the vessel wall.

check.q: What in a lymphatic vessel acts as a pump, and what cells start the contractions?
check.a: Valved chambers in the vessel wall act as pumps. Pacemaker cells in the chamber smooth muscle start the contractions.

steps.title: Skeletal muscle and thoracic pressure
steps.text:
2. Contraction of skeletal muscles. Surrounding muscle compresses lymphatic vessels and milks lymph along, the same idea as the muscle pump for veins. Valves stop it going backward.

3. Thoracic pressure changes. Breathing changes pressure in the thoracic cavity and that pressure change moves lymph toward the heart. Inspiration lowers thoracic pressure; lymph is drawn into the chest, just as venous blood is.

So lymph flow rises with walking and with breathing. Sitting still slows it, which is one reason oedema is worse after a long period of standing without movement (Chapter 21 already showed that for veins).
steps.mnemonic: V-M-T: Vessel wall (pacemakers), Muscle pump, Thoracic pressure.

check.q: Name the three ways lymph is moved through lymphatic vessels.
check.a: Contraction of the lymphatic vessels themselves (pacemaker-driven chambers), compression by skeletal muscle, and thoracic pressure changes of breathing.

steps.title: Where the lymph is heading
steps.text:
Lymph in these vessels is heading toward the thorax, where trunks and ducts empty it into the great veins near the heart (next lesson). The drainage diagram shows how lymphatic territories return fluid to the veins.

The lymphatic trunks and ducts model shows where it all ends: the trunks gather into the thoracic duct and the right lymphatic duct, which empty into the venous angles where the internal jugular and subclavian veins meet (next lesson).

check.q: Lymphatic vessels carry lymph toward which organ, and do they have a central pump?
check.a: Toward the heart (into thoracic veins). There is no central lymphatic pump.

practice.q: Compared with blood capillaries, lymphatic capillaries…
choices: Are less permeable and have a thick basement membrane
Are more permeable and lack a basement membrane
Have fenestrations and a continuous basement membrane
practice.why: More permeable, no basement membrane, one-way endothelial flaps.

practice.q: Which tissue DOES have lymphatic capillaries?
practice.why: Absent from nervous system, marrow, cartilage, cornea, epidermis. Dermis has them.

practice.q: Lymphatic capillaries are absent from all of the following EXCEPT…
practice.why: The liver has lymphatics. The listed absences are nervous system, marrow, cartilage, cornea, epidermis.

practice.q: Superficial lymphatic vessels tend to follow…
practice.why: Superficial follow veins; deep follow arteries.

practice.q: Lymphatic vessels most resemble which blood vessels?
practice.why: Structure similar to small veins, including valves.

practice.q: Lymph is moved by all of the following EXCEPT…
choices: A lymphatic heart in the mediastinum
practice.why: There is no central lymphatic pump.

practice.q: Why do overlapping endothelial cells of a lymphatic capillary act as one-way valves?
practice.a: Higher pressure outside opens the flaps and fluid enters; higher pressure inside closes them so lymph cannot leak back.

practice.q: Name the three tissues without blood vessels that also lack lymphatics.
practice.a: Cartilage, cornea, and epidermis.

practice.q: Put the path in order, starting in the tissues.

title: Five trunks and two ducts
summary: The five lymphatic trunks and their territories, then right lymphatic duct versus thoracic duct.
objectives: Name the five lymphatic trunks and the body region each drains
State what the right lymphatic duct drains
State what the thoracic duct drains
Say where ducts empty (into major veins of the thorax)
takeaways: Five trunks: jugular (head and neck); subclavian (upper limbs, superficial thoracic wall, mammary glands); bronchomediastinal (deep thoracic organs and wall); intestinal (abdominal organs); lumbar (lower limbs, pelvic and abdominal walls, pelvic organs).
Trunks empty into large thoracic veins or into lymphatic ducts.
Right lymphatic duct: right head, right upper limb, right thorax.
Thoracic duct: the remainder of the body.

steps.title: Vessels join into trunks
steps.text:
Lymphatic vessels drain into larger lymphatic trunks. A trunk is named for the territory it drains, not for a single organ. There are five. Learn the list with the territory beside each name; that pairing is the exam question.

Trunks then either empty into large veins in the thorax or into one of the two lymphatic ducts, which move lymph into those major veins. Either way, lymph rejoins blood near the heart.

The lymphatic trunks and ducts model draws them all on the atlas body, with the great veins, aorta, oesophagus and spine around them. Follow each trunk to its duct and into the veins; the drainage diagram below the text maps the territories.

check.q: What do lymphatic trunks empty into?
check.a: Either large veins in the thorax, or lymphatic ducts that then empty into those veins.

steps.title: Jugular, subclavian, bronchomediastinal
steps.text:
The three trunks of the neck and thorax:

Jugular trunk drains the head and neck.

Subclavian trunk drains the upper limbs, the superficial thoracic wall, and the mammary glands. Breast lymph therefore rides the subclavian trunk, which is why the axillary nodes matter clinically.

Bronchomediastinal trunk drains the deep thoracic organs and the deep thoracic wall (lungs, heart region, deep chest wall), not the skin of the chest.

On the model, the jugular trunks run down beside the internal jugular veins, the subclavian trunks along the subclavian veins, and the bronchomediastinal trunks climb out of the chest, all meeting at the root of the neck.
steps.mnemonic: Jugular = jaw/neck. Subclavian = under the clavicle (arm + breast). Bronchomediastinal = deep chest.

check.q: What does the subclavian trunk drain?
check.a: Upper limbs, superficial thoracic wall, and mammary glands.

steps.title: Intestinal and lumbar trunks
steps.text:
The two trunks below the diaphragm:

Intestinal trunk drains the abdominal organs (gut, and with them the chyle from lacteals). There is one intestinal trunk in the midline, not a left-right pair like the others.

Lumbar trunk (paired) drains the lower limbs, the pelvic and abdominal walls, and the pelvic organs.

Gut lymph feeds the intestinal trunk via lacteals.

On the model, all three empty into the cisterna chyli, the sac in front of L1–L2, to the right of the aorta, where the thoracic duct begins.

check.q: What does the intestinal trunk drain, and what does a lumbar trunk drain?
check.a: Intestinal: abdominal organs. Lumbar: lower limbs, pelvic and abdominal walls, and pelvic organs.

steps.title: Right lymphatic duct: one quarter of the body
steps.text:
There are two ducts. The smaller one is the right lymphatic duct.

It drains only the right side of the head, the right upper limb, and the right thorax. That is roughly the upper-right quarter of the body.

Everything else goes to the other duct. People reverse this on exams: they think “right duct = right half of the body.” It is not. The abdomen, both lower limbs, and the entire left side (head, arm, thorax) are not right-duct territory.

On the model, the right lymphatic duct is the short teal vessel entering the right venous angle, where the right internal jugular and subclavian veins meet; its three trunks (teal) join it there.
steps.pitfall: Right lymphatic duct = right head, right arm, right thorax ONLY. Not the right abdomen or right leg.

check.q: Which three regions does the right lymphatic duct drain?
check.a: Right side of the head, right upper limb, and right thorax.

steps.title: Thoracic duct: everything else
steps.text:
The thoracic duct drains the remainder of the body: the left head and neck, left upper limb, left thorax, and the entire body below the thorax (both sides of the abdomen, pelvis, and both lower limbs), including all the chyle from the intestinal trunk.

Both ducts empty lymph into major veins of the thorax, returning it to the blood just before the heart. The thoracic duct empties into the left venous angle (left internal jugular plus left subclavian vein).

On the model, follow it from the cisterna chyli up through the aortic hiatus, between the aorta and the azygos vein on the front of the spine (behind the oesophagus), across to the left at about T4–T5 and over the top into the left venous angle. The view “Whole system, from behind” hides the spine.

check.q: What does the thoracic duct drain?
check.a: The remainder of the body: everything not drained by the right lymphatic duct.

steps.title: A territory drill
steps.text:
Test yourself. Lymph from the right thumb: right lymphatic duct. Lymph from the left thumb: thoracic duct. Lymph from the right foot: thoracic duct (lumbar trunk, then thoracic duct). Lymph from the intestine (chyle): intestinal trunk, then thoracic duct. Lymph from the right breast: subclavian trunk on the right, then right lymphatic duct.

If you can place those five, you have the ducts.

On the model, the colours carry the answer: teal is the right lymphatic duct’s territory, green the thoracic duct’s. The right lumbar trunk is green.

check.q: A tumour cell leaving the right foot in lymph will next reach which duct?
check.a: The thoracic duct (via a lumbar trunk). The right lymphatic duct does not drain the lower limb.

practice.q: Which trunk drains the head and neck?
practice.why: Jugular trunk drains head and neck.

practice.q: Mammary glands drain via which trunk?
practice.why: Subclavian trunk: upper limbs, superficial thoracic wall, mammary glands.

practice.q: Deep thoracic organs drain via the…
practice.why: Bronchomediastinal trunk drains deep thoracic organs and deep thoracic wall.

practice.q: The right lymphatic duct drains all of the following EXCEPT…
practice.why: Right lower limb goes via a lumbar trunk into the thoracic duct.

practice.q: Chyle from the intestines reaches the blood via the…
practice.why: Intestinal trunk drains abdominal organs; that lymph joins the thoracic duct.

practice.q: Lymphatic ducts empty lymph into…
practice.why: Ducts move lymph into major thoracic veins.

practice.q: Name the five lymphatic trunks.
practice.a: Jugular, subclavian, bronchomediastinal, intestinal, lumbar.

practice.q: State the territory of the thoracic duct in one sentence.
practice.a: It drains the remainder of the body (everything the right lymphatic duct does not).

practice.q: Match body regions to the usual duct, going from right-duct territory to thoracic-duct territory.
items: Right head, right upper limb, right thorax (right lymphatic duct)
Left head, left upper limb, left thorax (thoracic duct)
Abdomen, pelvis, both lower limbs (thoracic duct)

title: Primary organs, secondary organs and MALT
summary: Where lymphocytes become immunocompetent, where they meet antigen, and the reticular-fibre filter shared by lymphatic tissue.
objectives: Name the primary lymphatic organs and what 'immunocompetent' means
Name the secondary lymphatic organs and tissues
Distinguish encapsulated organs from non-encapsulated tissue (MALT)
State what reticular fibres do in lymphatic tissue
takeaways: Primary (red bone marrow and thymus): where lymphocytes become immunocompetent (able to launch an immune response). Pre-B cells in marrow; pre-T cells in thymus.
Secondary: nodules (tonsils), diffuse lymphatic tissue, lymph nodes, spleen. Here lymphocytes meet each other, other immune cells, microbes and foreign substances.
Organs are encapsulated (CT capsule); tissue is not. Non-encapsulated tissue along mucosae is MALT.
Reticular cells make fine collagen reticular fibres that trap microorganisms and particles.

steps.title: Lymphatic tissue is a mix of cells
steps.text:
Lymphatic organs contain lymphatic tissue: lymphocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, reticular cells and other cells, sitting on a mesh of fibres.

Two questions organise the whole topic. Where does a lymphocyte learn its job? (primary organs). Where does it meet the antigen it was trained for? (secondary organs and tissues).

If you mix those two answers on an exam, every later question about nodes, spleen and MALT will go wrong.

check.q: What kinds of cells make up lymphatic tissue?
check.a: Lymphocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, reticular cells and other cells.

steps.title: Primary organs: red bone marrow and thymus
steps.text:
Primary lymphatic organs are red bone marrow and the thymus. This is where lymphocytes become immunocompetent: capable of launching an immune response.

Pre-B cells become immunocompetent in red bone marrow. The bone-marrow slide shows it: crowded blood-forming cells between fat cells. (The Compact Bone model also has a red-marrow cavity, if you want it in 3D.)

Pre-T cells leave the marrow still immature and become immunocompetent in the thymus (lesson 7). Find the thymus in the superior mediastinum, behind the sternum.

check.q: Where do pre-B cells and pre-T cells become immunocompetent?
check.a: Pre-B cells in red bone marrow; pre-T cells in the thymus.

steps.title: What immunocompetent means
steps.text:
An immunocompetent lymphocyte can recognise antigen and launch an immune response. That ability is not present at birth of the cell; it is trained in the primary organ.

Training includes learning to ignore the body's own molecules (tolerance, lesson 13). Cells that fail are deleted. The survivors are released into blood and colonise secondary organs, where they wait for their antigen.

The thymus histology shows packed cortical lymphocytes: that density is the training school.

check.q: What does immunocompetent mean?
check.a: Capable of launching an immune response (able to recognise antigen and respond).

steps.title: Secondary organs: where lymphocytes meet antigen
steps.text:
Secondary lymphatic organs are nodules (tonsils), diffuse lymphatic tissue, lymph nodes and the spleen.

These are the locations where lymphocytes interact with each other, with other immune cells, with microorganisms and with other foreign substances to produce an immune response. The meeting is the point.

Look at the spleen (blood-borne antigen) and the palatine tonsil (antigen from the mouth and nose). Node histology is in the next lesson and the spleen and tonsil slides follow; in each one you will see the same family resemblance: lymphocytes on a reticular mesh.

check.q: Name the secondary lymphatic organs and tissues.
check.a: Nodules (tonsils), diffuse lymphatic tissue, lymph nodes, and spleen.

steps.title: Capsule versus no capsule: organs versus tissue, and MALT
steps.text:
Lymphatic organs are encapsulated (a connective-tissue capsule). Lymphatic tissue is non-encapsulated.

Non-encapsulated lymphatic tissue is often associated with mucous membranes lining the digestive, respiratory, urinary and reproductive tracts. That tissue is called mucosa-associated lymphatic tissue (MALT).

The palatine tonsil is MALT you can see in the atlas. So are Peyer patches in the ileum (lesson 8). The tonsil histology is a nodule under epithelium, not a fully encapsulated organ like a node.
steps.pitfall: Tonsils are often listed with organs, but lecture classifies them as nodules (non-encapsulated MALT) among the secondary tissues.

check.q: What is MALT, and how does lymphatic tissue differ from a lymphatic organ?
check.a: MALT is mucosa-associated lymphatic tissue along digestive, respiratory, urinary and reproductive mucosae. Organs have a CT capsule; tissue does not.

steps.title: Reticular fibres, diffuse tissue and nodules
steps.text:
Both tissues and organs contain fine collagen reticular fibres produced by reticular cells. The fibres act as a filter to trap microorganisms and other particles, the way a net traps fish.

Diffuse lymphatic tissue: dispersed lymphocytes and macrophages; it blends with other tissues and is associated with other lymphatic tissue.

Lymphatic nodules: denser aggregations. They are numerous in the loose CT of digestive (including Peyer patches), respiratory, urinary and reproductive systems (MALT). When the same dense balls sit inside lymph nodes and spleen they are called lymphatic follicles.

The reticular-CT slide is the fibre mesh itself; the lymph-node slide shows follicles in place.

check.q: What do reticular fibres do, and when is a nodule called a follicle?
check.a: They trap microorganisms and particles. Nodules are called lymphatic follicles when they are found in lymph nodes and spleen.

steps.title: Put the map in your head
steps.text:
Primary = school (marrow, thymus). Secondary = workplace (nodes, spleen, tonsils, diffuse tissue). MALT = workplace built into a wet surface. Reticular fibres = the net.

Next three lessons are the named organs: node, spleen, thymus, then tonsils and Peyer patches.

check.q: Which two organs are primary, and why?
check.a: Red bone marrow and thymus, because that is where lymphocytes become immunocompetent.

practice.q: The primary lymphatic organs are…
practice.why: Primary = marrow (B) and thymus (T).

practice.q: Pre-T cells become immunocompetent in the…
practice.why: Pre-T cells mature in the thymus; pre-B cells in marrow.

practice.q: Immunocompetent means a lymphocyte can…
practice.why: Capable of launching an immune response.

practice.q: Which is a secondary lymphatic organ?
practice.why: Spleen is secondary. Marrow and thymus are primary.

practice.q: MALT is found along mucosae of the…
choices: Digestive, respiratory, urinary and reproductive tracts
practice.why: All four wet tracts.

practice.q: Reticular fibres in lymphatic tissue…
choices: Form a basement membrane for capillaries
practice.why: Fine collagen fibres produced by reticular cells act as a filter.

practice.q: Are lymphatic organs encapsulated or not, and what about lymphatic tissue?
practice.a: Organs are encapsulated (CT); tissue is non-encapsulated.

practice.q: When are lymphatic nodules called follicles?
practice.a: When they are found in lymph nodes and spleen.

practice.q: Put the lymphocyte's life in order.
items: Become immunocompetent in marrow (B) or thymus (T)
Meet antigen and mount a response

title: Lymph nodes: the filter on the pipe
summary: Bean-shaped filters on lymphatic vessels: capsule, cortex, medulla, more afferent than efferent, and why cancer cells lodge here.
objectives: Describe the size, shape and capsule of a lymph node
Distinguish cortex from medulla and name the supporting fibres
Explain why there are more afferent than efferent vessels
Say what happens to trapped substances, including cancer cells
takeaways: Nodes are 1-25 mm, round or bean-shaped, superficial or deep, with a dense CT capsule and trabeculae; reticular fibres form the supporting network.
Organised into cortex and medulla. More afferent vessels than efferent, so lymph slows and is filtered.
Substances are removed by phagocytosis or they stimulate lymphocytes to proliferate.
Cancer cells often migrate to nodes, become trapped and proliferate; they can then reach the blood (metastasis).

steps.title: What a lymph node is
steps.text:
A lymph node is a small, round or bean-shaped filter, 1-25 mm long, sitting on a lymphatic vessel. Superficial nodes lie near the skin; deep nodes lie beside viscera and vessels.

The job: filter lymph and destroy foreign substances. Everything that left the tissues in lymph must pass at least one node before it is returned to blood.

The 3D model is a whole node cut through its hilum. Rotate it. Match what you see to capsule, cortex and medulla rather than every labelled internal part.

check.q: How big is a lymph node, and what does it do?
check.a: About 1-25 mm, round or bean-shaped; it filters lymph and destroys foreign substances.

steps.title: Capsule, trabeculae, cortex and medulla
steps.text:
A dense connective-tissue capsule wraps the node. Trabeculae extend inward from the capsule and partly divide the interior. Reticular fibres form the supporting network that actually traps particles.

The interior is organised into a cortex (outer) and a medulla (inner). Lymphocytes are packed in both; the cortex holds the denser nodules/follicles.

On the model, find the capsule and its trabeculae, the outer cortex with its follicles (B cells), the paracortex (T cells) and the medullary cords toward the hilum. In the Lymph node slide (Histology tab) the same layout is the exam picture: dark cortex under a capsule, paler medulla toward the hilum.

check.q: Name the two regions inside a lymph node and the two connective-tissue supports.
check.a: Cortex and medulla. Capsule with trabeculae, plus a reticular-fibre network.

steps.title: More afferent than efferent
steps.text:
Several afferent lymphatic vessels pierce the convex surface and pour lymph in. Fewer efferent vessels leave at the hilum (the indented side), carrying filtered lymph out.

More in than out is deliberate. Lymph slows inside the sinuses, so macrophages have time to phagocytose debris and lymphocytes have time to inspect antigen.

Afferent = toward the node. Efferent = away.

On the model, follow lymph in through the afferent vessels on the convex surface, along the subcapsular and medullary sinuses, and out through the single efferent vessel at the hilum.
steps.pitfall: Afferent vessels are more numerous. Students often reverse afferent/efferent.

check.q: Why does a node have more afferent than efferent lymphatic vessels?
check.a: So lymph slows inside the node and can be filtered before it leaves.

steps.title: What happens to trapped substances
steps.text:
Two fates. Phagocytosis: macrophages eat the particle and destroy it. Or the substance stimulates lymphocytes to proliferate: a clone expands, and that is the start of an adaptive response (later lessons).

Lymph that leaves in the efferent vessel is cleaner than the lymph that entered, and it may now carry antibodies and activated lymphocytes downstream.

On the model, the macrophages lining the sinuses do the phagocytosis; the germinal centres of the follicles are where activated B cells proliferate.

check.q: What two things can happen to substances trapped in a lymph node?
check.a: They are removed by phagocytosis, or they stimulate lymphocytes to proliferate.

steps.title: Cancer cells and metastasis
steps.text:
Cancer cells often migrate into lymph, reach a node, become trapped and proliferate there. That is why a surgeon feels for enlarged, hard, painless nodes.

From the lymphatic system, cells can move into the circulatory system during metastasis: node to efferent lymph to duct to vein to blood to a distant organ.

A node that filters well is also a waypoint on the metastatic road.
steps.clinical: Hard, fixed, painless nodes are a warning. Tender mobile nodes are more often infection.

check.q: How can a cancer cell in a lymph node reach the blood?
check.a: It can leave in efferent lymph, enter a lymphatic duct, empty into a thoracic vein, and so enter the circulatory system (metastasis).

steps.title: Superficial versus deep
steps.text:
Nodes come in superficial groups, near the skin of the neck, axilla and groin (the ones you can feel when they swell), and deep groups along the great vessels and viscera of the chest and abdomen. In the atlas, find the cervical, axillary and inguinal nodes (superficial) and the mediastinal and abdominal nodes (deep).

Draw from memory: capsule, cortex, medulla; many afferent in, few efferent out; filter by phagocytosis or lymphocyte proliferation; a trap that metastases use.

check.q: Are lymph nodes only found near the skin?
check.a: No. There are superficial (near skin) and deep nodes.

practice.q: A typical lymph node is…
choices: A fat pad with no lymphocytes
practice.why: 1-25 mm, round/bean-shaped, encapsulated.

practice.q: Compared with efferent lymphatic vessels, afferent vessels of a node are…
practice.why: More afferent than efferent, so lymph slows and is filtered.

practice.q: The supporting network inside a node is made of…
practice.why: Reticular fibres form the supporting network.

practice.q: Substances trapped in a node are…
choices: Removed by phagocytosis or they stimulate lymphocytes to proliferate
practice.why: Phagocytosis or lymphocyte proliferation.

practice.q: Cancer cells trapped in nodes can…
choices: Proliferate and later enter the blood during metastasis
practice.why: They proliferate in the node and can reach the circulatory system.

practice.q: A lymph node is organised into…
choices: Cortex and medulla, with a dense CT capsule
practice.why: Cortex and medulla under a dense CT capsule.

practice.q: Why does lymph slow down inside a node?
practice.a: More afferent vessels than efferent, so lymph spends time in the sinuses being filtered.

practice.q: What wraps a lymph node, and what inward extensions does that wrapping send?
practice.a: A dense CT capsule; trabeculae extend inward.

practice.q: Put lymph's path through a node in order.
items: Efferent lymphatic vessel(s) at the hilum

title: The spleen: blood filter on the left
summary: Left superior abdomen, rupture risk, and four functions including destruction of defective red cells.
objectives: Locate the spleen and explain why rupture is dangerous
Describe the tissue that fills it (macrophages, red cells, enlarged capillaries, PALS, nodules)
List the four functions of the spleen
Identify erythrocytes as the cells the spleen destroys when they are defective
takeaways: Left superior abdomen. Traumatic rupture causes bleeding, shock, death.
Fibrous network filled with macrophages, RBCs and enlarged capillaries that connect to veins. Periarterial lymphatic sheath and lymphatic nodules hold lymphocytes and macrophages.
Four functions: destroy defective RBCs and recycle components (iron); detect and respond to foreign substances; limited blood reservoir; store and release platelets.
Nodes filter lymph; spleen filters blood.

steps.title: Where it sits, and why rupture kills
steps.text:
The spleen lies on the left superior side of the abdomen, tucked under the left ribs and diaphragm, lateral to the stomach. Find it in the atlas and rotate until you see how close it is to the rib cage.

It can be ruptured in traumatic abdominal injuries, resulting in bleeding, shock and death. The capsule is thin and the interior is a blood-filled sponge, so it bleeds briskly into the peritoneum.

There is no 3D model of the spleen's inside; the next steps use the histology slide for that. Here, the atlas organ is the thing to find, with the splenic artery that brings it blood and the splenic vein that drains it to the portal vein.
steps.clinical: Left-lower rib fractures and blunt trauma to the left upper quadrant are the classic setting for splenic rupture.

check.q: Where is the spleen, and why is rupture lethal?
check.a: Left superior abdomen. Rupture causes bleeding, shock and death.

steps.title: What it is made of
steps.text:
The spleen is a fibrous network filled with macrophages, red blood cells and enlarged capillaries that connect to veins. Blood is forced through that maze.

Around the arteries, a periarterial lymphatic sheath (PALS) and lymphatic nodules contain lymphocytes and macrophages. That is the immune side: antigen in the blood meets lymphocytes here.

The histology slide shows the capsule and the mixed pulp. Compare it with a lymph node: a node filters lymph arriving in afferent vessels; the spleen filters blood arriving in the splenic artery (shown with the spleen in the first step).

check.q: What two lymphatic structures around splenic arteries contain lymphocytes and macrophages?
check.a: The periarterial lymphatic sheath and lymphatic nodules.

steps.title: Function 1: destroy defective red cells
steps.text:
The spleen destroys defective RBCs and recycles their components, especially iron.

A red cell lives about 120 days (Lab 3). When it is old, stiff, or misshapen it cannot squeeze through the enlarged capillaries and is eaten by macrophages. Iron is salvaged for new haemoglobin in marrow.

On the blood-cell model, find the erythrocytes: anucleate biconcave discs, flexible enough to fold through narrow gaps. An old cell loses that flexibility, and that is what the spleen detects.

check.q: What does the spleen do to defective red blood cells?
check.a: It destroys them and recycles components such as iron.

steps.title: Function 2: detect and respond to foreign substances
steps.text:
Because blood is flowing through a mesh of lymphocytes and macrophages, the spleen detects and responds to foreign substances in the blood. Encapsulated bacteria in the bloodstream are a classic target.

This is the same job a node does for lymph. If you have no spleen, blood-borne antigen is less well seen, which is why lecture will later mention vaccination after splenectomy in other courses; here, remember the function: detect and respond.

check.q: How does the spleen participate in defense?
check.a: It detects and responds to foreign substances in the blood.

steps.title: Functions 3 and 4: reservoir and platelets
steps.text:
Limited reservoir for blood. The sponge can hold a little extra volume and return it. It is limited; do not picture a spare litre sitting there.

Stores and releases platelets. Platelets are the fragments you met in Lab 3. A pool of them sits in the spleen and can be released into blood.

Four functions. Recite them until they are automatic: destroy defective RBCs (recycle iron); detect and respond to foreign substances; limited blood reservoir; store and release platelets.
steps.mnemonic: D-D-R-P: Destroy RBCs, Detect antigen, Reservoir, Platelets.

check.q: List the four functions of the spleen.
check.a: Destroy defective RBCs and recycle components (iron); detect and respond to foreign substances; limited reservoir for blood; store and release platelets.

steps.title: Spleen versus node, one more time
steps.text:
Node: on a lymphatic vessel, filters lymph, more afferent than efferent. Spleen: in the left upper abdomen, filters blood, culls red cells, holds platelets.

Both have lymphocytes on a reticular/fibrous mesh. Both are secondary organs. Only the spleen handles worn-out erythrocytes as a named lecture function.
steps.pitfall: The spleen filters BLOOD, not lymph. Swap this with nodes and you lose two questions.

check.q: Which organ filters lymph, and which filters blood?
check.a: Lymph nodes filter lymph; the spleen filters blood.

practice.q: The spleen is located…
practice.why: Left superior side of the abdomen.

practice.q: Rupture of the spleen can cause…
practice.why: Traumatic rupture results in bleeding, shock, death.

practice.q: Which is NOT a lecture function of the spleen?
choices: Destroy defective RBCs and recycle iron
Detect and respond to foreign substances
Make all of the body's bile
practice.why: Bile is a liver product. The four spleen functions are RBC destruction, defense, reservoir, platelets.

practice.q: The periarterial lymphatic sheath of the spleen contains…
practice.why: PALS and lymphatic nodules contain lymphocytes and macrophages.

practice.q: Defective erythrocytes are destroyed mainly by…
practice.why: Spleen destroys defective RBCs and recycles iron.

practice.q: Compared with a lymph node, the spleen filters…
practice.why: Spleen filters blood; nodes filter lymph.

practice.q: Name the four functions of the spleen.
practice.a: Destroy defective RBCs and recycle components (iron); detect and respond to foreign substances; limited blood reservoir; store and release platelets.

practice.q: What fills the fibrous network of the spleen?
practice.a: Macrophages, red blood cells, and enlarged capillaries that connect to veins.

practice.q: Put the spleen facts in the order lecture presents them: location, danger, then the four functions.
items: Detect and respond to foreign substances

title: The thymus: T-cell school in the mediastinum
summary: Bilobed gland in the superior mediastinum, its size over a lifetime, cortex versus medulla with thymic corpuscles, and thymosin.
objectives: Locate the thymus and describe its two lobes and capsule
State how thymic size changes from year one to age 60 and after
Contrast cortex and medulla, including thymic corpuscles
Name the hormone that supports T-cell development
takeaways: Bilobed gland in the superior mediastinum. Capsule with trabeculae dividing lobes into lobules.
Increases in size in the first year of life, stays about the same until age 60, then decreases.
Cortex: many lymphocytes. Medulla: fewer lymphocytes but many thymic corpuscles (development of regulatory T cells).
Site of T-cell maturation. Secretes thymosin for T-cell development.

steps.title: Bilobed, in the superior mediastinum
steps.text:
The thymus is a bilobed gland in the superior mediastinum. In the atlas it sits behind the sternum, in front of the great vessels, above the heart. Two lobes, left and right.

A capsule surrounds each lobe. Trabeculae extend into the gland and divide it into lobules. That architecture (capsule → trabeculae → lobules) is the same idea as a lymph node, but the thymus has no afferent lymphatics bringing in antigen: it is a school, not a filter.

check.q: Where is the thymus, and how many lobes does it have?
check.a: Superior mediastinum; it is bilobed.

steps.title: Size across a lifetime
steps.text:
Lecture is specific, and it is not the 'biggest at puberty then involutes' line you may have heard elsewhere. Learn this version.

The thymus increases in size in the first year of life and remains the same size until 60, then it decreases in size.

Aging of immunity (last lesson of this chapter) starts here: a smaller thymus later in life means fewer new T cells.

Size versus function: the textbook aging section also describes replacement by fat and reduced new T-cell production before age 60. The size statement must not be read as preserved function until 60.
steps.pitfall: Distinguish the lecture’s gross-size description from declining functional thymic tissue and T-cell output.

check.q: How does thymic size change from birth to old age in this lecture?
check.a: It increases in the first year, remains the same size until age 60, then decreases.

steps.title: Cortex: packed with lymphocytes
steps.text:
Each lobule has a dark cortex and a paler medulla (the histology slide makes this obvious).

The cortex has many lymphocytes. These are developing T cells (thymocytes) being selected. Density is the point: lots of cells in training.

check.q: Which region of a thymic lobule has many lymphocytes?
check.a: The cortex.

steps.title: Medulla: fewer lymphocytes, thymic corpuscles
steps.text:
The medulla has fewer lymphocytes but many thymic corpuscles (Hassall's corpuscles in many atlases; lecture says thymic corpuscles).

Thymic corpuscles are involved in the development of regulatory T cells, the cells that later help keep the immune system from attacking self (tolerance, lesson 14).

So cortex = lots of developing T cells. Medulla = fewer lymphocytes, corpuscles, regulatory-T development.

check.q: What does the thymic medulla contain that the cortex does not emphasise, and what are those structures for?
check.a: Many thymic corpuscles, involved in development of regulatory T cells.

steps.title: T-cell maturation and thymosin
steps.text:
The thymus is the site of maturation of T cells. Pre-T cells arrive from marrow; immunocompetent T cells leave for secondary organs.

The gland secretes thymosin, a hormone used for T-cell development. Hormone plus the epithelial microenvironment of cortex and medulla together raise a T-cell repertoire.

No B-cell maturation here. B cells finish in marrow. Mix those two and Table 22.4 (later) falls apart.

check.q: What hormone does the thymus secrete, and what is it for?
check.a: Thymosin, for T-cell development.

steps.title: Thymus versus the other mediastinal organs
steps.text:
Heart: pump (Chapter 20). Thymus: T-cell school, sitting in the same mediastinum, in front of the great vessels. They are neighbours, not synonyms.

Spleen is in the abdomen. Nodes are scattered. Only the thymus is the primary organ in the chest.

check.q: Which primary lymphatic organ sits in the superior mediastinum?
check.a: The thymus.

practice.q: The thymus is…
choices: A bilobed gland in the superior mediastinum
A node on the thoracic duct
practice.why: Bilobed gland in the superior mediastinum.

practice.q: According to this lecture, thymic size…
choices: Peaks at puberty then involutes immediately
Increases in the first year, stays the same until 60, then decreases
practice.why: Up in year one, same until 60, then down.

practice.q: The thymic cortex is packed with…
practice.why: Cortex: many lymphocytes.

practice.q: Thymic corpuscles are found in the…
practice.why: Medulla has fewer lymphocytes but many thymic corpuscles.

practice.q: Thymic corpuscles are involved in development of…
practice.why: Development of regulatory T cells.

practice.q: Thymosin is secreted by the thymus for…
practice.why: Thymosin for T-cell development.

practice.q: What divides thymic lobes into lobules?
practice.a: A capsule with trabeculae extending into the gland.

practice.q: Where do T cells mature?
practice.a: The thymus.

practice.q: Put thymic regions from outside to inside of a lobule.

title: Tonsils, Waldeyer's ring and Peyer's patches
summary: The ring of tonsils at the mouth-pharynx border, plus Peyer patches in the ileum and the appendix as MALT.
objectives: Name the three tonsils of Waldeyer's ring and their common names
State the job of tonsillar crypts
Locate Peyer's patches and list their three jobs
Identify palatine tonsil, ileum and vermiform appendix in the atlas
takeaways: Tonsils: groups of lymphatic nodules in nasopharynx and oral cavity. Crypts trap bacteria and other harmful material.
Waldeyer's ring at the oral-pharynx border: palatine ('tonsils'), pharyngeal ('adenoids'), lingual.
Peyer's patches in the ileum: destroy bacteria, prevent breach of the intestinal wall, generate lymphocyte memory.
Appendix is MALT you can find in the atlas alongside the ileum.

steps.title: Tonsils: nodules with crypts
steps.text:
Tonsils are groups of lymphatic nodules in the nasopharynx and oral cavity. They are MALT: non-encapsulated (or incompletely encapsulated) lymphoid tissue under epithelium.

They protect against bacteria and other harmful material. The epithelium dips in as tonsillar crypts, pits that trap incoming microbes so lymphocytes underneath can meet them. Crypts are why tonsils look pitted, and why debris can sit in them.

The palatine tonsil is the one this atlas names. The histology slide shows crypts lined by epithelium with lymphoid nodules beside them.

check.q: What are tonsillar crypts for?
check.a: They trap bacteria and other harmful material so the lymphoid tissue can respond.

steps.title: Waldeyer's ring: three named tonsils
steps.text:
The tonsils form a ring (Waldeyer's ring) around the border between the oral cavity and the pharynx. Three names:

Palatine tonsils: the ones people call 'the tonsils'. Paired, in the oropharynx, visible when you say 'ah'. This is the atlas structure.

Pharyngeal tonsil: the one people call 'adenoids', in the nasopharynx. Enlarged adenoids block the nasal airway.

Lingual tonsil: on the posterior third of the tongue. The atlas shows the palatine tonsils; the pharyngeal and lingual tonsils are not separate atlas pieces.

Ring = palatine + pharyngeal + lingual. That list is the exam.

check.q: Name the three tonsils of Waldeyer's ring and the everyday names of the first two.
check.a: Palatine ('the tonsils'), pharyngeal ('adenoids'), lingual.

steps.title: Find the palatine tonsil
steps.text:
In the atlas, isolate the palatine tonsil. It sits in the tonsillar fossa between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches (those arches are not verified names here, so just find the tonsil itself).

This is the tonsil removed in tonsillectomy. It is also the one that is red and swollen in a typical sore throat.

check.q: Which tonsil is the one commonly called 'the tonsils'?
check.a: The palatine tonsils.

steps.title: Peyer's patches in the ileum
steps.text:
Peyer's patches are lymphatic nodules in the ileum (the last part of the small intestine). They are MALT of the gut: dense aggregations in the loose CT of the digestive tract (lesson 4).

Three jobs from lecture: destroy bacteria, prevent breach of the intestinal wall, and generate lymphocyte memory.

The ileum slide shows the patches as dark lymphoid aggregates in the mucosa and submucosa, on the side of the wall opposite the mesentery. (In the atlas the ileum is part of the small intestine and is not a separate piece.)

check.q: Where are Peyer's patches, and what three jobs do they have?
check.a: In the ileum. Destroy bacteria, prevent breach of the intestinal wall, generate lymphocyte memory.

steps.title: Vermiform appendix: more gut MALT
steps.text:
The vermiform appendix hangs from the caecum and is packed with lymphatic nodules. Lecture listed it with the gut MALT neighbourhood. On the ileocaecal model, find the appendix hanging from the caecum just below the terminal ileum, and the lymphoid follicles crowding its wall.

Same idea as Peyer patches: a sample of intestinal contents meets lymphocytes. Appendicitis is inflammation of this structure; that clinical name is extra colour, not a required lecture mechanism.

check.q: The vermiform appendix is a concentration of which kind of lymphatic tissue?
check.a: MALT (mucosa-associated lymphatic tissue) of the gut.

steps.title: A ring at each end of the gut tube
steps.text:
Waldeyer's ring guards the entrance (mouth and nose into the pharynx). Peyer's patches and the appendix guard the ileum and caecum. Both are secondary lymphatic tissue, not primary organs. T and B cells that trained in thymus and marrow work here.

You now have the organ list: nodes, spleen, thymus, tonsils, Peyer. Next is immunity itself, starting with barriers that never need a lymphocyte.

check.q: Are tonsils and Peyer's patches primary or secondary lymphatic tissue?
check.a: Secondary (MALT / nodules). Primary organs are marrow and thymus.

practice.q: Waldeyer's ring includes all EXCEPT…
practice.why: Peyer's patches are in the ileum, not in Waldeyer's ring.

practice.q: Adenoids are the…
practice.why: Pharyngeal tonsil = adenoids.

practice.q: 'The tonsils' in everyday speech are the…
practice.why: Palatine = 'tonsils'.

practice.q: Tonsillar crypts…
choices: Trap bacteria and other harmful material
practice.why: Crypts trap incoming harmful material.

practice.q: Peyer's patches are located in the…
practice.why: Ileum.

practice.q: Which is NOT a lecture job of Peyer's patches?
choices: Prevent breach of the intestinal wall
practice.why: T-cell maturation is the thymus.

practice.q: Name the three tonsils of Waldeyer's ring.
practice.a: Palatine, pharyngeal, lingual.

practice.q: What three things do Peyer's patches do?
practice.a: Destroy bacteria, prevent breach of the intestinal wall, generate lymphocyte memory.

practice.q: Put these MALT sites in order from the mouth toward the large intestine.

title: Three lines of defense: the barriers
summary: Innate versus adaptive, then the first line: skin pH 3-5, stomach pH 1-2, lysozyme, mucus and cilia.
objectives: Distinguish the three lines of defense and say which are innate
List surface chemicals of the first line
Give the pH of skin and of stomach and say why that matters
Explain lysozyme, mucus and cilia as barriers
takeaways: Innate = non-specific, does not discriminate. First line = physical barriers. Second line = internal defenses. Adaptive = third line: specific, slower, has memory.
Skin pH 3-5 plus sebum toxins. Stomach pH 1-2 plus protein-digesting enzymes. Vagina: low pH from normal flora.
Lysozyme in tears and saliva. Mucus traps particles in GI and respiratory tracts; cilia send them to the GI tract.
Secretions of the first line also include acids (HCl), saliva, sebum, mucus.

steps.title: Three lines of defense
steps.text:
From here the chapter is immunity. Start with the split.

Innate defenses are non-specific: they do not discriminate between substances. They are already in place. Two of the three lines are innate: the first line is physical barriers (this lesson); the second line is internal defenses (chemicals, inflammation, white cells: next two lessons).

Adaptive defenses fight specific foreign substances. They take longer to mobilise but they give memory. That is the third line: antigens, B cells, antibodies, T cells (lessons 12-15).

check.q: Which lines of defense are innate, and what is different about the third line?
check.a: First (barriers) and second (internal) are innate and non-specific. The third is adaptive: specific, slower, has memory.

steps.title: Skin: pH 3-5 and sebum
steps.text:
The first line is the surface. Skin is inhospitable to bacteria because of its low pH (3-5) and because sebum contains toxins. Tight keratinised epithelium is a physical wall; the acid film is a chemical wall.

The thin-skin slide is that wall: epidermis with no lymphatics (lesson 2) but plenty of barrier. pH 3-5 is the number to memorise; it is not as acidic as stomach, but it is acidic enough that many bacteria fail.

check.q: What is the pH of the skin, and what oily secretion adds toxins?
check.a: pH 3-5; sebum contains toxins that are inhospitable to bacteria.

steps.title: Stomach: pH 1-2
steps.text:
The stomach is a killing chamber. Very low pH (1-2) neutralises bacteria, and protein-digesting enzymes (pepsin) destroy proteins of microbes that swallowed acid did not already kill.

Find the stomach on the histology slide. HCl is the acid named among first-line secretions (acids, saliva, sebum, mucus).

pH 1-2 versus skin 3-5: do not swap them.
steps.pitfall: Skin 3-5, stomach 1-2. Stomach is far more acidic.

check.q: What is gastric pH, and what else in the stomach kills microbes?
check.a: pH 1-2, which neutralises bacteria, plus protein-digesting enzymes.

steps.title: Vagina, tears, saliva: flora and lysozyme
steps.text:
The vagina has low pH because of acid produced by the normal flora of the reproductive tract. Wipe out that flora (broad-spectrum antibiotics) and yeast can overgrow: a lecture aside ('yeast infections?').

Tears contain enzymes with antimicrobial properties, especially lysozyme. Saliva has antibacterial chemicals, again including lysozyme. Lysozyme is the named enzyme of the first line; it also appears among 'surface chemicals' in the next lesson's mediator list.

check.q: Where is lysozyme found in the first line of defense?
check.a: In tears and saliva (antimicrobial enzymes / antibacterial chemicals).

steps.title: Mucus and cilia of the GI and respiratory tracts
steps.text:
In the GI and respiratory tracts, foreign particles are trapped in mucus and sent to the GI tract by cilia (the mucociliary escalator of the airway dumps trapped dirt into the throat to be swallowed, where stomach acid finishes the job).

The nasal-mucosa slide shows a ciliated, mucus-producing surface. That is first-line architecture, not an immune cell.

check.q: How do the GI and respiratory tracts use mucus and cilia as a barrier?
check.a: Mucus traps foreign particles; cilia send them to the GI tract.

steps.title: Why 'innate' and 'non-specific' both matter
steps.text:
These barriers do not need to have seen the microbe before, and they do not care whether it is bacterium A or virus B: acid is acid. That is innate and non-specific.

They also have no memory. Living in a sterile bubble would atrophy adaptive immunity; it would not stop skin pH from being 3-5.

When a microbe gets through, the second line (complement, interferons, inflammation, phagocytes, NK cells) starts. That is the next lesson.

check.q: Why are barriers called innate and non-specific?
check.a: They are always present and they do not discriminate between substances (no antigen specificity, no memory).

practice.q: The first line of defense is…
practice.why: First line = physical barriers (and their chemicals).

practice.q: Adaptive immunity is the…
practice.why: Third line: specific, slower, memory.

practice.q: Skin pH is about…
practice.why: Skin 3-5; stomach 1-2.

practice.q: Stomach pH is about…
practice.why: Very low pH (1-2) plus protein-digesting enzymes.

practice.q: Lysozyme is an antimicrobial enzyme in…
practice.why: Tears and saliva.

practice.q: Vaginal low pH is maintained by…
practice.why: Normal flora of the reproductive tract.

practice.q: Name four first-line secretions listed in lecture.
practice.a: Acids (HCl), saliva, sebum, mucus.

practice.q: What do mucus and cilia do in the respiratory tract?
practice.a: Mucus traps particles; cilia send them to the GI tract.

practice.q: Put the three lines of defense in order.
items: Adaptive immunity (B cells, T cells, memory)

title: Complement, interferons and inflammation
summary: The second line's chemicals: complement (MAC, opsonization, chemotaxis), interferons, and local versus systemic inflammation.
objectives: Name the two complement pathways and the three things activated complement can do
Explain how interferons protect neighbouring cells
List the vessel changes of inflammation and the five local signs
Contrast local with systemic inflammation
takeaways: Complement: ~20 inactive blood proteins (C1-C9 and factors B, D, P). Alternative (innate, C3 binds foreign substance) vs classical (adaptive, needs antibody on antigen).
Activated complement: MAC (lysis), opsonization (coat for phagocytosis), chemotaxis (attract cells, promote inflammation).
Interferons: virus-infected cell warns neighbours, which make antiviral proteins; too late for the cell that made the interferon.
Local: redness, heat, swelling, pain, loss of function. Systemic: those plus neutrophilia, fever (pyrogens), and in severe cases widespread leak → shock/death.

steps.title: Chemical mediators of innate immunity
steps.text:
Once a barrier is breached, chemicals run the second line. Lecture's list: surface chemicals (lysozyme in tears and saliva, already done); histamine and kinins (vasodilation and increased vascular permeability in inflammation); interferons (viral defense); complement (inflammation and killing microbes); prostaglandins and leukotrienes (promote inflammation); pyrogens (fever); cytokines (proteins cells secrete that bind receptors on other cells and stimulate a response).

Three of these get full diagrams: complement, interferon, inflammation.

check.q: Name three chemical mediators that promote inflammation.
check.a: Histamine and kinins; prostaglandins and leukotrienes; complement (also pyrogens for fever).

steps.title: Complement: two pathways into one cascade
steps.text:
Complement is a group of about 20 inactive proteins that circulate in blood (C1-C9 and factors B, D, P). They activate each other in a cascade.

Alternative pathway (innate): C3 binds a foreign substance and attracts macrophages. No antibody needed.

Classical pathway (adaptive): requires antibodies bound to antigens. So complement is listed with innate immunity, but one of its on-switches is an adaptive product. That overlap is intentional.

check.q: What starts the alternative pathway versus the classical pathway of complement?
check.a: Alternative: C3 binds a foreign substance (innate). Classical: antibodies bound to antigens (adaptive).

steps.title: What activated complement does: MAC, opsonization, chemotaxis
steps.text:
Three named effects. Learn all three.

Membrane attack complex (MAC): complement proteins form a channel through the plasma membrane of the microbe → cell lysis.

Opsonization: complement proteins attach to the surface of bacterial cells and stimulate phagocytosis (make the bacterium tasty).

Chemotaxis: attract immune-system cells to the site of infection and so promote inflammation.

check.q: Name the three effects of activated complement.
check.a: MAC (lysis), opsonization (phagocytosis), chemotaxis (attract cells / promote inflammation).

steps.title: Interferons: the infected cell warns its neighbours
steps.text:
Interferons are proteins that protect against viral infection and some cancers.

A virus-infected cell produces interferons that cannot aid the infected cell but can bind to surfaces of neighbouring cells and stimulate production of antiviral proteins that stop viral replication.

Altruism at cell scale: too late for me, in time for you. This is innate, not antigen-specific.

check.q: Can the interferon made by an infected cell save that same cell? What does it do instead?
check.a: No. It binds neighbouring cells and tells them to make antiviral proteins that stop viral replication.

steps.title: Inflammation: three vessel changes
steps.text:
Inflammation results from many types of tissue injury. Chemical mediators produce:

Vasodilation (more blood: redness and heat). Positive chemotaxis (cells crawl toward the cue). Increased vascular permeability, which lets fibrinogen and complement enter the tissue. Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin and isolates the infected area (a wall).

Local inflammation is confined to a specific body area. Signs: redness, heat, swelling, pain, loss of function.

check.q: Name the three vessel-level events of inflammation, and the five local signs.
check.a: Vasodilation, positive chemotaxis, increased vascular permeability. Signs: redness, heat, swelling, pain, loss of function.

steps.title: Systemic inflammation: neutrophils, fever, shock
steps.text:
Systemic inflammation occurs in many parts of the body. Same signs as local, plus:

An increase in neutrophil concentration as cells are released by red bone marrow.

Fever: pyrogens produced by various cells; fever improves the immune response.

In severe cases, widespread increase in vascular permeability (histamines): a large volume of plasma enters interstitial spaces → shock and death. That is the same leak that is useful when it is local, and lethal when it is everywhere.
steps.clinical: Systemic capillary leak can drop blood volume enough to cause shock. Local fibrin isolation is the useful version of the same permeability change.

check.q: What three extras distinguish systemic from local inflammation?
check.a: Neutrophilia (marrow release), fever (pyrogens), and in severe cases widespread vascular leak that can cause shock/death.

steps.title: Tie the chemicals to the vessels
steps.text:
Histamine and kinins: vasodilation and leak. Complement: MAC, opsonize, call cells, also feed inflammation. Interferons: antiviral neighbourhood watch. Pyrogens: fever. Prostaglandins and leukotrienes: more inflammation.

White cells that answer the chemotactic call are the next lesson.

check.q: Which complement pathway requires antibody, and which does not?
check.a: Classical requires antibody on antigen; alternative does not (C3 binds the foreign substance).

practice.q: The alternative complement pathway is part of…
choices: Innate immunity (C3 binds a foreign substance)
practice.why: Alternative = innate; C3 binds foreign substance.

practice.q: The classical complement pathway requires…
choices: C3 binding a foreign substance without antibody
practice.why: Classical = adaptive; needs antibody on antigen.

practice.q: A membrane attack complex…
choices: Forms a channel in the microbe's plasma membrane and lyses it
practice.why: MAC = channel → cell lysis.

practice.q: Opsonization means complement proteins…
choices: Attach to bacteria and stimulate phagocytosis
practice.why: Coat the bacterium → phagocytosis.

practice.q: Interferons protect…
choices: The already-infected cell that made them
Neighbouring cells, which then make antiviral proteins
practice.why: Too late for the producer; neighbours make antiviral proteins.

practice.q: Systemic inflammation can kill because…
choices: Fever always denatures all body protein instantly
Widespread vascular permeability lets a large volume of plasma leave the blood (shock)
practice.why: Histamine-driven leak of plasma into tissues → shock/death.

practice.q: List the five local signs of inflammation.
practice.a: Redness, heat, swelling, pain, loss of function.

practice.q: What does increased vascular permeability allow into the tissue, and what does fibrin do?
practice.a: Fibrinogen and complement enter; fibrinogen becomes fibrin and isolates the infected area.

practice.q: Put complement's three effects in the order MAC, then coat, then call.

title: Innate immune cells: recognition, recruitment and killing
summary: Follow a white cell from a chemotactic signal to a target, then distinguish the cells in Table 22.2.
objectives: Explain chemotaxis and phagocytosis
Match each innate cell to its job
Distinguish NK cells from antigen-specific T cells
takeaways: Neutrophils arrive early; macrophages sustain phagocytosis and repair.
Basophils and mast cells release inflammatory mediators; eosinophils defend against parasites.
NK cells are innate lymphocytes that kill abnormal cells without a clone-specific antigen receptor.

steps.title: Chemotaxis brings cells to the problem
steps.text:
Chemotaxis is directed movement along a chemical gradient. Microbial products and signals from injured tissue or other immune cells attract leukocytes. Recruitment is different from killing: a cell must first leave blood and reach the affected tissue.

The blood model distinguishes a multilobed neutrophil from a monocyte with an indented nucleus. These shapes help you identify the cells; their functions explain why they are recruited.

check.q: How does chemotaxis differ from phagocytosis?
check.a: Chemotaxis guides movement toward a signal; phagocytosis engulfs and destroys a target.

steps.title: Phagocytosis: attach, engulf, digest
steps.text:
Phagocytosis is endocytosis and destruction of a target by a phagocyte; the lecture names neutrophils and macrophages. In order:

• Adherence to the target must occur first.

• The target is enclosed in a vesicle that fuses with lysosomes, forming a phagolysosome, where acidification and lysosomal enzymes digest it.

• A respiratory burst makes oxidizing chemicals such as hydrogen peroxide that also kill it.

Antibody or complement coating makes adherence easier: that is opsonization, the bridge between recognizing a target and eating it.

check.q: Why does coating a bacterium with an opsonin help?
check.a: It improves recognition and attachment by phagocytes, making engulfment more effective.

steps.title: Neutrophils first; macrophages persist
steps.text:
Neutrophils are the first cells to enter infected tissue, and they live only a few hours there. They release cytokines and chemotactic factors that increase the inflammatory response and recruit and activate other immune cells. Their lysosomal enzymes (defensins) kill microorganisms but also damage tissue, which may produce pus. They can also cross the wall of the GI tract to protect it.

Macrophages are large free or fixed phagocytes: monocytes that have entered the tissues. They live longer than neutrophils, ingest larger particles, and produce interferons, prostaglandins and complement. They sit beneath free surfaces (skin, subcutaneous tissue, mucous and serous membranes) and in the sinuses of the spleen, bone marrow, liver and lymph nodes.

Names by tissue: in sinuses, reticuloendothelial cells; in the lungs, dust cells; in the liver, Kupffer cells; in the CNS, microglia. On the blood-cell model, compare the neutrophil’s multilobed nucleus with the monocyte’s kidney-shaped one (Table 22.2).

check.q: Which cell commonly arrives early, and which sustains cleanup?
check.a: Neutrophils arrive early; macrophages sustain phagocytosis, antigen presentation and repair.

steps.title: Granules, parasites and inflammation
steps.text:
Basophils and mast cells promote inflammation by releasing histamine and leukotrienes. Basophils are motile and enter infected tissues; mast cells are non-motile and stay in connective tissue.

Eosinophils enter tissues, reduce inflammation by degrading pro-inflammatory chemicals, and secrete enzymes that kill some parasites. (Table 22.2 adds that they also take part in the inflammation of asthma and allergies.)

On the blood-cell model, the basophil’s bilobed nucleus is hidden by large dark granules; the eosinophil has a bilobed nucleus and red-orange granules.

check.q: Which cells release histamine, and what two things do eosinophils do (lecture)?
check.a: Basophils and mast cells release histamine and leukotrienes. Eosinophils reduce inflammation by degrading pro-inflammatory chemicals and secrete enzymes that kill some parasites.

steps.title: Natural killer cells do not need clonal specificity
steps.text:
Natural killer (NK) cells are non-phagocytic lymphocytes of innate immunity. They lyse tumor and virus-infected cells, by triggering apoptosis and with perforins, and they enhance inflammation. They recognize classes of cells, not specific antigens, which is why they count as innate.

Cytotoxic T cells also kill virus-infected and tumor cells, but a cytotoxic T-cell clone recognizes one particular peptide on MHC I. Same outcome, different recognition. On the blood-cell model, NK cells have the shape of the large (granular) lymphocyte.

check.q: Why is an NK cell innate even though it is a lymphocyte?
check.a: Its recognition is not based on the antigen-specific, clonally selected receptor used by B and T cells.

practice.q: Which cell is usually an early phagocyte at an infected wound?
practice.why: Neutrophils are rapidly recruited innate phagocytes.

practice.q: A tissue-resident cell releases histamine. Which is the best match?
practice.why: Mast cells reside in connective tissue and release inflammatory mediators.

practice.q: Which cell is especially associated with parasite defense?
practice.why: Eosinophil granule products can damage parasites.

practice.q: An NK cell kills a tumor cell. Which statement is correct?
choices: It must first become a plasma cell
practice.why: NK cells are lymphocytes, but belong to innate immunity.

practice.q: Arrange the main phagocytic events.
Name the macrophages associated with lung, liver and CNS.
practice.a: Alveolar macrophages (dust cells), Kupffer cells, and microglia.

practice.q: In the lungs, macrophages are called…
practice.why: Lungs: dust cells. Liver: Kupffer cells. CNS: microglia. Sinuses: reticuloendothelial cells.

title: Adaptive immunity: antigens, epitopes and receptors
summary: Build the vocabulary needed for antigen recognition before learning activation.
objectives: Distinguish innate recognition from adaptive specificity and memory
Define antigen, hapten and epitope
Compare B-cell and T-cell receptors
takeaways: B cells mediate antibody responses; T cells mediate cellular responses and regulation.
An epitope is the part recognized, not necessarily the whole antigen.
A hapten needs a carrier to elicit an immune response.

steps.title: Recognize, respond and remember
steps.text:
Adaptive immunity targets particular antigens and leaves memory cells. On first exposure, a matching rare lymphocyte must be activated and expanded, so the response takes time. Re-exposure can recruit an existing memory population.

B cells produce plasma cells that secrete antibodies. T cells include cytotoxic, helper and regulatory populations. Innate defenses start earlier and help activate these adaptive responses; the two systems cooperate.

check.q: What three verbs summarize adaptive immunity?
check.a: Recognize a particular antigen, respond to it, and remember it.

steps.title: Antigens and haptens
steps.text:
An antigen is a large molecule that stimulates an immune response. Foreign antigens come from an external source: bacteria, viruses and other disease-causing microorganisms, and also pollen, animal dander, feces of mites, foods and drugs.

A hapten is a small molecule that stimulates an immune response only when attached to body proteins. That is why a small drug bound to one of your own proteins can become a new immune target (penicillin allergy is the classic example).

check.q: What makes a hapten different from an independently immunogenic antigen?
check.a: A hapten needs attachment to a carrier to elicit the response.

steps.title: Self markers, tumor targets and tolerance
steps.text:
Self-antigens are molecules produced by the body and used as markers to tell self from non-self. Normally tolerance stops the immune system from attacking them.

The lecture gives one benefit and one danger. Benefit: a response to tumor antigens (altered self) can destroy cancer cells. Danger: a response to normal self causes tissue destruction: autoimmunity.

Keep autoimmunity separate from allergy, which is a harmful response to a harmless external antigen.

check.q: How do autoimmunity and allergy differ?
check.a: Autoimmunity targets self; allergy is a harmful response to an external antigen.

steps.title: One antigen can carry several epitopes
steps.text:
An epitope, or antigenic determinant, is the particular region recognized by an antigen receptor. A large antigen may carry several different epitopes, so multiple lymphocyte clones may respond to the same organism or protein.

Members of one clone share receptor specificity. The antigen selects a matching clone from a pre-existing repertoire; it does not teach every lymphocyte to make the same new receptor.

check.q: Can different clones respond to one large antigen?
check.a: Yes. Different clones may recognize different epitopes on it.

steps.title: B and T receptors recognize differently
steps.text:
A B-cell receptor is membrane immunoglobulin: two heavy and two light polypeptide chains make two matching antigen-binding sites. It can bind intact antigen.

A typical T-cell receptor has two chains with variable and constant regions. It recognizes a peptide displayed by an appropriate MHC molecule, rather than binding free intact antigen like an antibody. The schematic receptors in the blood model illustrate the distinction, not molecular scale.

check.q: Which receptor can bind intact antigen, and which recognizes peptide plus MHC?
check.a: B-cell receptor: intact antigen. T-cell receptor: peptide presented with MHC.

practice.q: The particular part of an antigen recognized by a receptor is the…
practice.why: Epitope and antigenic determinant are synonyms.

practice.q: A small chemical becomes immunogenic after binding a protein. It acts as a…
practice.why: A hapten requires a carrier.

practice.q: Which population gives rise to antibody-secreting plasma cells?
practice.why: Activated B cells can differentiate into plasma cells.

practice.q: What does a typical T-cell receptor recognize?
practice.why: Recognition involves the presented peptide and the MHC molecule.

practice.q: Why can a single protein activate several clones?
practice.a: It can contain several epitopes, each recognized by a different clone.

practice.q: What distinguishes adaptive memory from the initial response?
practice.a: Memory populations remain after activation and respond more rapidly to subsequent exposure.

title: MHC I and MHC II: where the antigen came from matters
summary: Trace intracellular and extracellular antigen along different presentation pathways.
objectives: Compare endogenous and exogenous antigens
Match MHC I to CD8 and MHC II to CD4
Explain why presentation does not automatically destroy a cell
takeaways: Most nucleated cells display intracellular peptides with MHC I to CD8 T cells.
