Professional antigen-presenting cells display ingested peptides with MHC II to CD4 helper T cells.
Normal self presentation is routine; activation and recognition context matter.

steps.title: The presentation window
steps.text:
MHC molecules hold peptide fragments at the cell surface. A T cell examines the peptide together with the MHC molecule. This reveals something about proteins inside the cell or material the cell has taken up.

The genes encoding MHC vary between individuals. A T-cell receptor must recognize its appropriate peptide in the appropriate self-MHC context: this is MHC restriction.

check.q: What two components does a T-cell receptor recognize in presentation?
check.a: The peptide and the presenting MHC molecule.

steps.title: MHC I displays the inside of a nucleated cell
steps.text:
Endogenous antigens are proteins the cell makes itself, through gene expression and protein synthesis: normal self proteins, viral proteins in an infected cell, or mutated proteins in a tumor cell.

MHC class I molecules are found on all nucleated cells. They display endogenous antigens and, when the displayed peptide is foreign, prompt immune cells to destroy the displaying cell: a cytotoxic (CD8) T cell recognizes it and kills the cell. Normal self peptides on MHC I are ignored.

Mature red blood cells have no nucleus, so they carry no MHC I.

check.q: Which pathway lets a cytotoxic T cell inspect a virus-infected cell?
check.a: Endogenous peptide on MHC I, recognized by a CD8 cytotoxic T cell.

steps.title: MHC II displays material taken up from outside
steps.text:
Exogenous antigens are substances taken in from the external environment by phagocytosis and broken down inside the cell.

MHC class II molecules display exogenous antigens on antigen-presenting cells (APCs): B cells, macrophages, monocytes and dendritic cells (in the skin, the dendritic cells are Langerhans cells).

A helper (CD4) T cell binds the MHC II–antigen complex. This presentation is MHC-restricted: the T cell needs both the antigen and the APC’s own MHC II. Unlike MHC I, it does not lead to destruction of the APC; it sends a signal that stimulates other immune cells to respond.

check.q: Which cells does the lecture list as antigen-presenting cells?
check.a: B cells, macrophages, monocytes and dendritic cells (Langerhans cells in the skin).

steps.title: From uptake to display
steps.text:
In the course pathway, a macrophage engulfs extracellular material, breaks it into fragments, associates a peptide with MHC II, and transports the complex to its surface. A matching helper T cell can now bind.

Display is a prerequisite, but full activation also requires additional signals. The next lessons distinguish antigen recognition from costimulation and from the later division of the activated clone.

check.q: Does peptide-MHC recognition alone guarantee full naive T-cell activation?
check.a: No. Appropriate costimulation and signaling context are also needed.

steps.title: Compare two infection locations
steps.text:
Imagine a bacterium engulfed by an APC and a virus synthesizing proteins inside another cell. The introductory comparison is ingested bacterium → MHC II → helper T, versus intracellular viral peptide → MHC I → cytotoxic T.

These are teaching pathways, not claims that real pathogens trigger only one arm of immunity. Antibodies can neutralize a virus before cell entry, while cytotoxic cells address already infected cells.

check.q: Why can antibodies and cytotoxic T cells both matter in a viral infection?
check.a: Antibodies act on extracellular virus; cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells.

practice.q: A viral protein made within a cell is an example of…
practice.why: It is synthesized inside the cell.

practice.q: MHC I is recognized by which principal effector type?
practice.why: CD8 T cells recognize peptides with MHC I.

practice.q: MHC II presentation primarily activates…
practice.why: MHC II is the helper-T presentation pathway.

practice.q: Which statement about MHC I is correct?
choices: It also presents normal self peptides
practice.why: Self presentation is normal; recognition of an abnormal target and effector context matter.

practice.q: Order the introductory MHC II pathway.
items: Peptide associates with MHC II and reaches the surface
Recognition by a matching helper T cell

practice.q: Contrast the usual outcomes of MHC I and MHC II recognition.
practice.a: MHC I can identify a target for cytotoxic killing; MHC II recruits helper-T coordination.

practice.q: Which cell is NOT one of the lecture’s antigen-presenting cells?
practice.why: APCs with MHC II: B cells, macrophages, monocytes and dendritic cells (Langerhans cells in the skin).

title: Clonal selection and tolerance: expand the right cells
summary: Separate lymphocyte development, antigen-driven expansion and protection against self attack.
objectives: Define clone, proliferation and differentiation
Distinguish developmental selection from clonal expansion
Describe three mechanisms of tolerance
takeaways: B cells mature in marrow; T cells mature in thymus.
Antigen selects an existing specific clone for expansion.
Deletion, failure of activation and regulatory T cells contribute to tolerance.

steps.title: Origin and maturation are different locations
steps.text:
B and T lymphocytes originate from precursors in red bone marrow. B cells mature there; T-cell precursors travel to the thymus. Immunocompetence means that a cell can mount an appropriate response, not that it has already fought its matching antigen.

Mature cells circulate through blood and secondary lymphatic tissues. Nodes and spleen bring them into contact with antigens and APCs.

check.q: Where do B and T cells originate and mature?
check.a: Both originate in marrow. B cells mature in marrow; T cells mature in thymus.

steps.title: Developmental positive and negative selection
steps.text:
The lecture’s two selections, in its own words:

Positive selection ensures the survival of lymphocytes that react against antigens; these proliferate and form clones.

Negative selection eliminates clones of lymphocytes that react against self-antigens.

(In the thymus, positive selection specifically keeps the T cells that can recognize the body’s own MHC molecules, and negative selection removes those that react too strongly to self. Either way: keep the useful ones, delete the dangerous ones.)

check.q: What do positive and negative selection do?
check.a: Positive selection keeps lymphocytes that react against antigens, so they can proliferate into clones; negative selection eliminates clones that react against self-antigens.

steps.title: An antigen selects a matching clone
steps.text:
A clone is a family of lymphocytes sharing antigen specificity. When a matching mature lymphocyte receives appropriate activation signals, it divides repeatedly: proliferation.

Some descendants specialize into effector cells and others persist as memory cells: differentiation. The response becomes large enough to work while keeping its original specificity.

check.q: What is the difference between proliferation and differentiation?
check.a: Proliferation increases cell number; differentiation changes cells into specialized functional types.

steps.title: Tolerance has several safeguards
steps.text:
Tolerance is immune unresponsiveness to a particular antigen, especially normal self. The course lists deletion of self-reactive cells, prevention of their activation and suppression by regulatory T cells.

Failure to receive the correct costimulation can make recognition ineffective rather than activating. Regulatory T cells add active suppression, including inhibitory cytokines. No single checkpoint perfectly describes the whole system.

check.q: Name three safeguards against self-directed lymphocyte responses.
check.a: Deletion, prevention of activation, and regulatory T-cell suppression.

steps.title: When control fails
steps.text:
Autoimmunity means an immune response injures self tissue. Immunodeficiency means defense is inadequate. Allergy is harmful reactivity to an external antigen. These are different failures, even though all involve immune regulation.

Regulatory T cells normally restrain B cells and other T cells. Removing all regulation would not simply make immunity better; it could increase tissue injury.

check.q: Why is lymphocyte inhibition useful?
check.a: It maintains tolerance and limits excessive or inappropriate tissue-damaging responses.

practice.q: Antigen-driven clonal expansion primarily increases…
practice.why: A matching clone proliferates.

practice.q: Which is a tolerance mechanism?
practice.why: Deletion helps prevent self attack.

practice.q: T cells mature in the…
practice.why: T precursors originate in marrow and mature in thymus.

practice.q: Becoming a plasma cell is an example of…
practice.why: Differentiation produces specialized cell function.

practice.q: Define a clone.
practice.a: A population descended from a lymphocyte that shares its antigen specificity.

practice.q: Why are developmental selection and an immune response not the same process?
practice.a: Selection establishes a useful, tolerized repertoire; a later antigen selects and expands a matching mature clone.

practice.q: In the lecture, positive selection…
choices: Ensures survival of lymphocytes that react against antigens
Eliminates lymphocytes that react against self-antigens
Turns B cells into plasma cells
practice.why: Positive selection keeps lymphocytes that react against antigens (they proliferate into clones); negative selection eliminates clones that react against self-antigens.

title: Helper T-cell activation and costimulation
summary: Connect antigen presentation to helper-T proliferation and then to B-cell and cytotoxic responses.
objectives: Explain recognition and costimulation
Identify B7 and CD28
Trace helper-T support of B cells and cytotoxic T cells
takeaways: Peptide-MHC recognition gives specificity; additional signals support activation.
B7 on the APC binds CD28 on the T cell.
Helper-T signals support both humoral and cellular responses.

steps.title: Signal one supplies specificity
steps.text:
An APC displays a processed peptide on MHC II. A helper T cell with a matching receptor binds the complex. Many passing T cells do not match and will not respond to this peptide.

Recognition selects the appropriate responder, but binding is not the complete activation story. This distinction helps keep random recognition of harmless material from automatically becoming a destructive response.

check.q: Which complex is recognized by the helper T-cell receptor?
check.a: A matching peptide presented on MHC II.

steps.title: Costimulation supplies the additional context
steps.text:
In the lecture example, B7 on the APC binds CD28 on the helper T cell. This is a costimulatory signal, not the antigen itself. Cytokines from the APC also influence the T-cell response.

The interaction therefore combines specific recognition with additional surface and soluble signals. Remember the direction of the named pair: APC B7 → T-cell CD28.

check.q: Where are B7 and CD28 in this interaction?
check.a: B7 is on the APC; CD28 is on the T cell.

steps.title: Proliferation makes enough helper cells
steps.text:
Activated helper T cells produce signals that promote expansion. The textbook example connects APC interleukin-1 and helper-T interleukin-2 with proliferation. The population grows from rare matching cells to many descendants.

Antigen recognition, costimulation and proliferation are sequential concepts: identify the target, receive the necessary context, then expand the response.

check.q: Why must the matching population proliferate?
check.a: Initially too few matching cells exist to mount a large effective response.

steps.title: Help for B cells
steps.text:
A B cell can bind antigen with its receptor, take it up and present a peptide on MHC II. An appropriate helper T cell supplies contact-dependent help and cytokines.

In the course pathway the activated B population produces plasma cells, which secrete antibodies, and memory B cells, which support a later response. Not every B-cell response has identical helper requirements, but this is the main pathway being taught.

check.q: Which B-cell descendants secrete antibody, and which remain for recall?
check.a: Plasma cells secrete antibody; memory B cells support later responses.

steps.title: Help for cytotoxic cells and a brake on the response
steps.text:
Helper-T cytokines also support cytotoxic T-cell activation and expansion. The cytotoxic cells do the target killing; helper cells coordinate the response.

Regulatory T cells restrain helper, B-cell and cytotoxic activity. Thus the same adaptive system contains accelerators and brakes. A question about which cell helps both branches is asking for helper T, not a plasma cell.

check.q: Which T-cell type coordinates both B and cytotoxic responses?
check.a: Helper T cells.

practice.q: B7 on an APC binds…
practice.why: B7-CD28 is the named costimulatory pair.

practice.q: The direct antibody-secreting effector is a…
practice.why: Plasma cells are differentiated B-cell effectors.

practice.q: Which cell supports both B-cell and cytotoxic-T responses?
practice.why: Helper T cells coordinate both adaptive arms.

practice.q: Arrange the helper-T activation pathway.
items: APC processes and displays peptide on MHC II
Matching helper T cell recognizes the complex
Costimulation and cytokine signals support activation
Helper T cells proliferate and support other lymphocytes

practice.q: Why is antigen recognition not synonymous with full activation?
practice.a: Full activation requires appropriate additional signals and cellular context.

practice.q: Contrast helper and regulatory T cells.
practice.a: Helper T cells promote responses; regulatory T cells inhibit inappropriate or excessive activity.

title: Antibody structure and the five immunoglobulin classes
summary: Use structure to understand antigen binding, then learn the distinguishing jobs of IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE and IgD.
objectives: Label heavy, light, variable and constant regions
Match all five classes to their major functions
Distinguish placental from milk antibody transfer
takeaways: A basic antibody unit contains two heavy and two light chains.
Variable regions bind antigen; constant regions recruit effector functions.
IgG crosses placenta; IgA protects mucosal surfaces; IgM appears early; IgE participates in allergy; IgD is a B-cell receptor.

steps.title: Four chains make a basic Y-shaped unit
steps.text:
An antibody is an immunoglobulin made by a plasma cell. Its basic unit has two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains. The arms contain matching antigen-binding regions.

Membrane immunoglobulin serves as a B-cell receptor. Secreted antibody can travel away from the cell that produced it. Do not confuse the producer, the receptor and the released protein.

check.q: How many heavy and light chains form a basic antibody unit?
check.a: Two heavy chains and two light chains.

steps.title: Variable recognizes; constant recruits
steps.text:
The variable regions at the arm tips determine antigen specificity. The constant region determines class and supports functions such as binding immune-cell receptors or activating complement.

Two antibodies can target different antigens while sharing an immunoglobulin class. Class and specificity answer different questions: what effector behavior is available, and what is being recognized?

check.q: Which region determines specificity, and which supports class-dependent effector functions?
check.a: Variable region: specificity. Constant region: class-dependent effector functions.

steps.title: IgG and IgM
steps.text:
IgG is the major serum class. It promotes opsonization and can activate complement. It crosses the placenta, providing passive protection to the fetus and newborn.

IgM is often the first secreted class in a primary response and is effective at complement activation. Secreted IgM is commonly pentameric, whereas B-cell surface IgM is monomeric. The course connects IgM with ABO transfusion reactions and IgG with Rh-related disease.

check.q: Which class crosses the placenta and which commonly appears first?
check.a: IgG crosses the placenta; IgM commonly appears first in a primary response.

steps.title: IgA, IgE and IgD
steps.text:
IgA protects mucosal surfaces and occurs in tears, saliva, colostrum and milk; secretory IgA is commonly a dimer. IgE binds mast cells and basophils and participates in allergic responses and parasite defense. IgD functions as an antigen receptor on naive B cells alongside IgM.

Study location with function: mucosal secretion suggests IgA; placental transfer suggests IgG; mast-cell sensitization suggests IgE.

check.q: Match secretions, mast cells and B-cell receptors to classes.
check.a: Secretions: IgA. Mast cells: IgE. B-cell receptors: IgD and IgM.

steps.title: Read Table 22.6 critically
steps.text:
The supplied table lists serum percentages of IgG 80–85%, IgM 5–10%, IgA 15%, IgE 0.002% and IgD 0.2%. Those entries do not form one internally consistent 100% sample, so use them as the course table values rather than adding them into a pie chart.

The robust comparison is that IgG predominates in serum while very low-abundance IgE can still cause strong effects. Mechanism and distribution are more informative than concentration alone.

check.q: Does low serum abundance imply weak biological effects?
check.a: No. IgE is scarce in serum but can trigger strong mast-cell responses.

practice.q: An antibody binding site lies in its…
practice.why: Variable regions confer specificity.

practice.q: The principal placentally transferred antibody class is…
practice.why: IgG crosses the placenta.

practice.q: Which class protects the infant through breast milk?
practice.why: Milk and colostrum contain protective IgA.

practice.q: Which class is often secreted first in a primary response?
practice.why: IgM commonly precedes a class-switched response.

practice.q: Which class binds mast cells in immediate allergy?
practice.why: IgE sensitizes mast cells and basophils.

practice.q: List the five immunoglobulin classes.
practice.a: IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE and IgD.

practice.q: How does secreted IgM differ structurally from surface IgM?
practice.a: Secreted IgM is commonly pentameric; B-cell surface IgM is monomeric.

title: What antibodies do, and why the second response is faster
summary: Connect neutralization, cross-linking, complement and opsonization with primary and secondary responses.
objectives: Contrast direct and indirect antibody effects
Explain primary versus secondary responses
Distinguish plasma cells from memory cells
takeaways: Antibodies can neutralize or cross-link targets and recruit other defenses.
IgG and IgM can activate classical complement.
Memory B cells make subsequent responses faster and generally stronger.

steps.title: Neutralization blocks a function
steps.text:
Binding an antigen can directly interfere with its action. An antibody may block a toxin-binding site or prevent a virus from attaching to a host cell. This is neutralization.

The antibody does not need to engulf anything. It prevents an interaction. This works especially well while the target is extracellular, before a toxin or virus has entered a cell.

check.q: How can an antibody protect without directly lysing a target?
check.a: By binding and blocking a needed interaction, such as toxin binding or viral attachment.

steps.title: Cross-linking gathers targets
steps.text:
Antibodies have multiple antigen-binding sites and can link compatible targets. Clumping particulate antigens is agglutination; forming complexes with soluble material can produce precipitation.

Visible clumps are useful in some laboratory tests. Cross-linking is not the same as making a membrane pore; it gathers antigens so they can be detected or cleared.

check.q: How do agglutination and precipitation differ?
check.a: Agglutination clumps particles or cells; precipitation forms insoluble complexes from soluble antigens.

steps.title: Complement and opsonization recruit partners
steps.text:
When suitable IgG or IgM binds antigen, its constant region can initiate the classical complement pathway. Complement can promote inflammation, coat targets and form membrane attack complexes.

IgG can also act as an opsonin: its antigen-binding portion attaches to the target and its constant portion is recognized by a phagocyte. Antibody provides the bridge; the phagocyte performs ingestion.

check.q: Who actually engulfs an antibody-coated bacterium?
check.a: A phagocyte; the antibody promotes recognition and attachment.

steps.title: IgE links recognition to mediator release
steps.text:
IgE attaches to mast-cell or basophil receptors through its constant region. A matching antigen can cross-link bound IgE and trigger release of mediators such as histamine.

That connects adaptive antigen specificity to inflammatory effects. Immediate hypersensitivity can involve this pathway; a delayed T-cell-mediated skin reaction is a different mechanism.

The lecture’s example is hay fever: inhaled antigens (usually plant pollen) combine with IgE on mast cells, which then release inflammatory chemicals such as histamine.

check.q: Why is an IgE-associated allergic response antigen-specific?
check.a: The IgE variable regions recognize the matching antigen, which triggers the sensitized cell.

steps.title: Primary response creates memory; secondary response uses it
steps.text:
The primary response begins with first exposure. Matching B cells expand and produce plasma cells and memory B cells; antibody takes time to rise.

The secondary response begins from established memory, so antibody typically rises sooner, reaches a higher level and persists longer. Memory cells are not simply long-lived free antibody: they are cells capable of mounting a renewed response.

check.q: What cellular change explains a faster response to a repeat antigen?
check.a: An expanded population of antigen-specific memory cells is already available.

practice.q: An antibody blocks a toxin from binding its receptor. This is…
practice.why: It prevents toxin function by binding.

practice.q: An antibody-coated bacterium is easier to ingest. This is…
practice.why: Opsonins improve phagocyte attachment.

practice.q: Which pair can initiate classical complement?
practice.why: Antigen-bound IgG or IgM can activate classical complement.

practice.q: Compared with a primary response, a secondary response is generally…
practice.why: Memory cells support a quicker, larger response.

practice.q: Explain agglutination without using the word lysis.
practice.a: Antibodies cross-link particulate targets into clumps.

practice.q: Why are memory cells different from circulating antibodies?
practice.a: Memory cells persist and can generate a new response; antibodies are proteins that eventually degrade.

title: Cell-mediated immunity: identify and remove an infected cell
summary: Trace cytotoxic recognition, killing and memory while comparing helper and NK cells.
objectives: Explain how cytotoxic T cells recognize targets
Describe perforin and target-cell death
Compare immediate antibody and delayed cellular hypersensitivity
takeaways: Cytotoxic T cells recognize specific peptide-MHC I complexes.
Killing an infected cell removes an intracellular replication site.
Helper, regulatory and memory T cells have different roles from cytotoxic effectors.

steps.title: When the pathogen is inside
steps.text:
Antibodies are most effective against accessible extracellular targets. Once a microbe is replicating inside a cell, removing the infected cell may be necessary. Cytotoxic T cells provide antigen-specific cellular killing.

The cell displays endogenous peptides on MHC I. A matching activated cytotoxic T cell can recognize an abnormal target; helper signals support the development of an effective response.

check.q: Why is cellular immunity important for intracellular infection?
check.a: It can identify and remove infected cells that shelter replicating microbes.

steps.title: Perforin, granzymes and programmed death
steps.text:
Cytotoxic T (Tc) cells work in two ways:

• They lyse virus-infected cells, tumor cells and tissue transplants: perforin forms a hole in the plasma membrane of the target cell (granzymes delivered through it then trigger apoptosis).

• They produce cytokines that promote phagocytosis and inflammation.

Memory T cells are produced too. The killing is aimed at a recognized target, not at every nearby cell.

check.q: What is the central outcome of cytotoxic granule delivery?
check.a: Death of the recognized target cell, commonly through apoptosis.

steps.title: Do not swap the T-cell jobs
steps.text:
Helper T cells coordinate and support responses. Cytotoxic T cells kill targets. Regulatory T cells restrain responses. Memory T cells persist and respond effectively at re-exposure.

All are T cells, but a question about antibody help is different from a question about killing a virus-infected epithelial cell. Use the requested action to choose the population.

check.q: Which T-cell types help, kill, restrain and remember?
check.a: Helper, cytotoxic, regulatory and memory T cells, respectively.

steps.title: Cytotoxic T versus natural killer
steps.text:
Both can kill abnormal cells. A cytotoxic T-cell clone recognizes a specific peptide-MHC I target after adaptive activation. NK cells use an innate balance of activating and inhibitory signals and do not use the same clone-specific T-cell receptor.

On the blood-cell model, compare a small T lymphocyte with a large (granular) lymphocyte, the shape most NK cells have. Shape cannot tell you which cell is antigen-specific; that is a question of receptors and mechanism, which is what the exam asks.

check.q: What distinguishes cytotoxic T-cell recognition from NK recognition?
check.a: Specific peptide-MHC I recognition by the T-cell receptor versus innate recognition signals.

steps.title: Cellular memory and delayed reactions
steps.text:
Some activated T cells become memory cells, improving future responses. T cells also mediate forms of delayed hypersensitivity, including contact responses that develop over days.

Compare that with rapid IgE-associated mediator release. Timing helps distinguish mechanisms in a teaching vignette, but timing alone does not identify every clinical cause.

check.q: Which adaptive arm is associated with delayed contact hypersensitivity?
check.a: Cell-mediated immunity involving T cells.

practice.q: An infected cell displays viral peptide on MHC I. The matching killer is a…
practice.why: Cytotoxic T cells recognize peptide-MHC I.

practice.q: Perforin and granzymes support…
practice.why: They are cytotoxic effector products.

practice.q: Which cell primarily restrains adaptive responses?
practice.why: Regulatory T cells help maintain tolerance and control.

practice.q: Delayed contact hypersensitivity primarily involves…
practice.why: Delayed cellular responses involve T cells.

practice.q: Why can a transplant provoke a cellular immune response?
practice.a: Recipient T cells may recognize donor-associated targets as foreign.

practice.q: Are all lymphocytes adaptive immune cells?
practice.a: No. NK cells are lymphocytes of innate immunity.

title: Active or passive, natural or artificial?
summary: Use two independent questions to classify the four forms of acquired immunity.
objectives: Classify all four acquired-immunity categories
Explain the timing and memory tradeoff
Distinguish antigen administration from antibody transfer
takeaways: Active means your immune system responds; passive means ready-made protection is transferred.
Natural versus artificial describes how exposure or transfer occurs.
Passive protection is rapid but does not itself generate recipient memory.

steps.title: Two axes, not four unrelated definitions
steps.text:
Immunization is deliberate exposure to an antigen or an antibody. To classify any immunity, ask two questions.

First ask who makes the immune response? Active immunity recruits the recipient’s own lymphocytes. Passive immunity supplies preformed antibodies or, in some settings, immune cells.

Then ask how did the exposure happen? Natural exposure occurs in ordinary biological circumstances; artificial exposure is deliberately provided. Combining the two answers gives the four categories.

check.q: What are the two classification questions?
check.a: Is protection actively produced or passively transferred, and is the route natural or deliberate?

steps.title: Active natural and active artificial
steps.text:
After natural infection, a person may retain antigen-specific memory: active natural immunity. A vaccine deliberately presents antigen or instructions for making antigen so the recipient mounts a response: active artificial immunity.

Both require the immune system to respond, and both can produce memory. The classification does not imply that natural infection is preferable; it only describes the route.

check.q: Why are both infection-associated immunity and vaccination active?
check.a: The recipient’s immune system makes the response and can form memory.

steps.title: Passive natural: mother to child
steps.text:
Maternal IgG crosses the placenta. Maternal IgA in colostrum and milk helps protect mucosal surfaces. The infant receives antibody made by someone else: passive natural immunity.

Protection wanes as transferred antibody is lost or degraded. Receiving antibody does not by itself create the infant’s own antigen-specific memory population.

check.q: Name the two maternal antibody routes and classes.
check.a: Placenta: IgG. Colostrum and milk: IgA.

steps.title: Passive artificial: supplied antibodies
steps.text:
Passive artificial immunity is the transfer of antibodies (or cells) from an immune animal to a nonimmune human: an antiserum. The lecture lists where it is available: rabies, hepatitis and measles; the toxins of tetanus, diphtheria and botulism; and the venoms of poisonous snakes and black widow spiders.

Its advantage is immediate protection; its limit is that it is temporary and does not make the recipient’s own memory cells.

check.q: What is the advantage and main limitation of transferred antibody?
check.a: Rapid protection, but it is temporary and does not itself produce recipient memory.

steps.title: Why a booster and antibody are different tools
steps.text:
A booster re-exposes an already primed immune system to antigen and recruits memory. A supplied antibody preparation acts immediately without waiting for the recipient to produce antibody.

In a textbook comparison, one supplies an immediate effector and the other supports a continuing active response. Keep the antigen-versus-antibody distinction clear whenever a question names an injection.

check.q: Is every injection an example of active artificial immunity?
check.a: No. Antigen-based vaccination is active; transferred antibody is passive artificial immunity.

practice.q: Memory following natural infection is…
practice.why: The recipient responds to natural antigen exposure.

practice.q: A vaccine that induces a recipient response is…
practice.why: Deliberate antigen exposure induces active immunity.

practice.q: Maternal IgG crossing the placenta is…
practice.why: Ready-made antibody is transferred naturally.

practice.q: Administered antivenom antibody is…
practice.why: Antibody is deliberately transferred.

practice.q: Why does passive antibody protection wane?
practice.a: Transferred antibodies degrade and do not themselves establish recipient memory.

practice.q: What makes a booster faster than an initial antigen exposure?
practice.a: Existing antigen-specific memory supports a secondary response.

title: Immunotherapy, aging and an integrated immune response
summary: Finish Chapter 22 by connecting immune activation, inhibition and age-related changes.
objectives: Explain activation and inhibition as immunotherapy strategies
Describe age-related loss of immune responsiveness
Trace cooperation between innate and adaptive defenses
takeaways: Immunotherapy may stimulate or inhibit immune function.
Thymic functional tissue and new T-cell output decline with age.
Aging affects response speed, magnitude and memory formation more than ordinary lymph fluid drainage.

steps.title: Immunotherapy can increase or decrease activity
steps.text:
Immunotherapy treats disease by changing immune function or directing immune products toward a target. Examples in the course include cytokines and monoclonal antibodies.

Activation can help mount a response against a tumor. Inhibition can reduce damaging immune activity. More immune activity is not automatically better; the desired direction depends on the disease mechanism.

check.q: Does immunotherapy always stimulate immunity?
check.a: No. It can activate, redirect or inhibit immune function.

steps.title: Monoclonal antibodies and checkpoints
steps.text:
A monoclonal antibody recognizes a defined target. Different therapeutic antibodies can mark a cell for destruction, block a signaling interaction or change immune regulation.

Checkpoint therapy can release an inhibitory brake on T cells. That can improve antitumor activity but can also disturb tolerance. The mechanism differs from simply supplying antimicrobial antibody for short-term passive protection.

check.q: Why can releasing an immune checkpoint have both benefit and harm?
check.a: It may strengthen tumor responses while also permitting unwanted immune injury.

steps.title: Thymic size is not the same as thymic function
steps.text:
The lecture describes early growth, approximately stable overall size until later adulthood, then shrinkage. The textbook’s aging section adds a crucial distinction: functional thymic tissue is progressively replaced by fat, and output of newly matured T cells falls earlier.

Thus an organ can retain an outline while losing functional tissue. Existing T cells can proliferate in secondary tissues, so reduced thymic output does not mean all circulating T cells suddenly disappear.

check.q: Why can declining thymic output coexist with a maintained circulating T-cell count?
check.a: Existing peripheral T cells can proliferate even while fewer new cells mature in the thymus.

steps.title: Responses become less effective with age
steps.text:
The lecture’s aging list: little effect on the lymphatic system’s ability to remove fluid from tissues; the thymus atrophies; primary and secondary responses decrease: more antigen is needed, the response is slower, less antibody is made and fewer memory cells are produced.

The ability of cell-mediated immunity to resist intracellular pathogens decreases (influenza is the example), latent pathogens can reactivate (herpes zoster: shingles), and autoimmune diseases and cancers increase.

check.q: Which declines more in this chapter’s comparison: routine lymph drainage or immune responsiveness?
check.a: Immune responsiveness.

steps.title: One tissue infection ties the chapter together
steps.text:
A barrier is breached. Innate mediators alter local vessels and recruit cells; phagocytes ingest material. Lymph carries tissue material toward nodes, where APCs and rare matching lymphocytes meet.

Helper signals support B-cell and cytotoxic responses. Antibodies act on accessible antigen; cytotoxic cells remove infected targets. Regulatory mechanisms limit injury, and memory cells remain. The sequence links vessels, organs, cells and molecules instead of treating them as separate lists.

check.q: Why are lymph nodes useful meeting places for adaptive activation?
check.a: They collect tissue-derived material and bring APCs together with circulating lymphocytes.

practice.q: Which statement about immunotherapy is correct?
choices: It can stimulate or inhibit immunity
practice.why: Therapeutic goals may require activation or inhibition.

practice.q: A monoclonal antibody is characterized by…
practice.why: It recognizes a defined target.

practice.q: With aging, new thymic T-cell output generally…
practice.why: Functional thymic tissue declines with age.

practice.q: Shingles illustrates…
practice.why: Reduced control can permit latent varicella-zoster reactivation.

practice.q: Why can immunotherapy require inhibition rather than stimulation?
practice.a: An excessive or self-directed immune response can cause disease.

practice.q: List three age-related immune changes from the course.
practice.a: Slower responses, less antibody production and reduced memory formation; impaired cellular defense is another example.
